A completed contract is not a failed commitment.

Yet somehow, in 2026, we're still treating project-based careers as a red flag.

I've had a few conversations with recruiters recently, and the same questions keep coming up:

"Why haven't you stayed at one company for 10 years?"

"Why have you worked with so many different organizations?"

Here's the thing: Not every career is built around permanent employment.

Much of my experience has been in consulting, fixed-term contracts, and project-based engagements across gaming, esports, commercial partnerships, marketing, and live events.

You join with a defined objective. You take ownership. You deliver. Sometimes the assignment ends, and you move on.

That's not necessarily job-hopping. That's how project-based work operates, i fucking hated sometimes absolutely but it puts food on the table.

I value autonomy, accountability, transparency, and straightforward communication. I want to work with people who care more about what gets delivered than how long someone has occupied the same desk.

And while LinkedIn is full of success stories, here's a less glamorous reality:

I've been looking for my next opportunity for a while. Recently, I signed a contract with a Saudi-based company. Two days later, they backed out, citing budget issues.

Two days. After signing. 

No motivational spin here. It's frustrating, and the market can be brutal.

But I'm still here, still building relationships, and still looking for the right opportunity.

I'm not looking for a company where I can simply collect years of tenure. I'm looking for one where I can contribute, challenge ideas constructively, take ownership, and create measurable value.

A question for hiring managers: When did tenure become a more important measure of someone's value than what they've actually delivered?

And to companies hiring in gaming, esports, partnerships, sponsorships, or commercial growth: I'm open to a meaningful conversation.💪🏽

Two Nordic AI data centre stories landed yesterday, and together they say a lot about where hiring is heading.

SWI Group raised €800 million at a €6.1 billion valuation. That's more than €1 billion of equity since March, backing AI campuses across the UK, Ireland and Europe, and the conversion of 1.3GW of former bitcoin mining sites in the US and Sweden.

On the same day, VivoPower started construction on a 40MW AI conversion at Mo i Rana in northern Norway. Local works are under way, and the specialist mechanical and electrical fit-out contract is due to be awarded shortly.

It's the same story twice: old powered sites are being turned into AI capacity, and fast. 

Money and power are in place, so the bottleneck is people. Critical-environment electricians, commissioning engineers, cooling specialists and project leads are all coming from the same small European pool.

6 days from a 30-minute briefing to an accepted offer.

My most recent recruitment assignment started on 30 September. There was no polished job description waiting for me. The client came to me with the role, the technical stack, and an idea of the person they needed. 
So we started with a 30-minute conversation. We covered the technical requirements, seniority, personality and team fit, salary budget, working model and, importantly, when they actually wanted this person to start. From there, I built the recruitment process.

This was my funnel: 
Role briefing → Job specification → Market mapping → Sourcing → Outreach → Screening → Shortlist → Client interviews → Verba Offer →Contract signed 

And this is where I think recruitment today becomes really interesting, because the process was a combination of technology, AI, automation, and human judgement.
I used Claude to help structure and refine the job description. I posted the role on my favourite job board, JustJoinIT, and yes, as always, I negotiated a good commercial deal with the consultant there. 
😉I used LinkedIn Recruiter and X-Ray searches to map the market and build the initial pipeline. Then I used Juicebox to expand the search and support candidate outreach.

But technology was only part of it. Behind those tools was a lot of searching, reviewing profiles, adjusting the search, understanding who was actually relevant and speaking to people. 

The numbers looked like this:
~800 profiles reached/identified
↓~300 candidates actively approached or reviewed through direct search and applications
↓12 screening conversations
↓4 candidates introduced to the client
↓2 invited to face-to-face interviews
↓1 offer
↓1 hire

The right candidate had their face-to-face interview on 5 October. The offer was made on 7 October. Time to hire: 10 days. And I’m particularly happy about this one because my historically short time-to-hire hasn’t disappeared as the tools around recruitment have changed. 

If anything, the tools make me faster. But they don’t decide which four people I should put in front of a hiring manager. They don’t understand the conversation behind a brief that doesn’t even have a job description yet. And they don’t build trust with a candidate who wasn’t necessarily planning to change jobs. That’s where the recruiter still matters. And this assignment was a great reminder of how much I enjoy working closely with clients, understanding what they really need, and helping them grow their teams quickly and effectively

YOUR NEXT CAREER OPPORTUNITY MAY BE IN A COUNTRY YOU'VE NEVER CONSIDERED.

We often search for jobs within familiar borders. But what if the geography of your search is limiting your opportunities?

According to Eurostat, unemployment across the EU stood at 6.1% in August 2026. Yet the differences between countries are significant:

→ Finland — 10.3%
→ Spain — 10.0%
→ Estonia — 8.0%
→ Germany — 4.0%
→ Poland — 3.4%
→ Czechia — 3.2%

These numbers don't tell us where the best jobs are. But they reveal something important: Europe is not one uniform labour market.

For professionals whose work can be delivered digitally — designers, developers, marketers, content creators and AI specialists — this raises an interesting question:

Why limit your job search to one country?

A broader international search can help you:

→ Discover companies and industries outside your local market.
→ Explore opportunities in economies with different hiring conditions.
→ Connect directly with international employers and decision-makers.
→ Consider remote employment, freelance contracts and project-based collaboration.

Of course, a low unemployment rate doesn't automatically mean more vacancies. And not every remote position allows cross-border employment.

Industry demand, language requirements, hiring regulations and the employer's remote-work policy matter just as much.

The goal isn't to chase the country with the lowest unemployment rate. It's to stop treating your local job market as the limit of your professional opportunities.

🎬 Two judgments in two days, one national enforcement law and a VLOP designation ruling due on 14 October: a new episode of 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁(𝘀) 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 is out.

🇮🇹 Italy names its AI Act enforcers
Law No. 177 sets out which authorities will enforce the AI Act in Italy. Market surveillance authorities and financial oversight institutions, including the Bank of Italy and the financial markets supervisor, are called to assess the declared risks of high-risk AI systems, while data protection authorities are kept in the loop and participate within the limits of their mandate. The law also bans fully automated HR decisions on hiring, dismissal, disciplinary measures and performance reviews. A complex mechanism that will only work if those authorities cooperate in practice.

📄 Zalando v Commission (T-203/24)
On 7 October 2026, the General Court dismissed Zalando’s challenge to the Commission’s refusal to disclose the documents used to calculate its DSA supervisory fee, holding that the Commission lawfully relied on the protection of third-party commercial interests and ongoing judicial proceedings. The judgment marks the limits of transparency around the methodologies and datasets behind VLOP supervision.

📞 Digi România and Investcapital (C-872/24 and C-909/24)
On 8 October 2026, the Court confirmed that late-payment penalty clauses in telecom contracts may be declared unfair under the Unfair Terms Directive, even where national telecom rules impose no cap. Once a clause is found unfair, national courts must disapply it entirely rather than reduce the amount.

👀 Already on the calendar
On 14 October 2026, the General Court rules in Technius v Commission (T-134/24), on whether the Commission correctly calculated the average monthly active recipients behind a VLOP designation, and whether it may rely on third-party estimates rather than the platform’s own figures.

A persistent narrative suggests that artificial intelligence will spark widespread job displacement and contract technology operations. But actual enterprise hiring data reveals a very different reality: AI is not eliminating Global Capability Centers (GCCs)—it is permanently changing what they hire for. 
Rather than signaling industry contraction, AI-driven automation is shifting workforce requirements away from high-volume transactional roles toward high-density engineering, system design, and AI orchestration.

#FutureOfWork #GCC #AI #TechHiring #HRTech #AgenticAI #TalentAcquisition #Leadership #IndiaTech

If you work in software consulting, you've probably heard it by now: AI is going to kill time & material.

I think it's true. And it's happening faster than most people expect.

For years we've sold software the same way. More people, more hours, bigger invoice.

But a small senior team with AI agents can now do work that used to take 20 people a year. Migrations, testing, legacy rewrites. That's exactly the work time & material was built on.

So what changes?

→ Clients will pay for outcomes, not hours. A small, sharp team charging more for less time will beat a big team billing by the day.
→ Engineers will split. People who just copy-paste requests into an AI become easy to replace. People who make the calls on architecture and quality become worth a lot more.
→ Vendors will earn less revenue but better margins. Middle layers with no real expertise will get squeezed out.
→ Buyers need to level up. If you can't judge a partner, or you won't share your real business goals with them, you'll get average results.

The smartest clients we work with are already doing this. Before they sign a big contract, they build a working version of the idea in MonstarX and put it in front of real users. By the time they talk scope, they know what's worth building.

One more thing. Cutting juniors because "AI can do it" is a mistake. Every senior was a junior once. Stop hiring them now and you won't have seniors in five years.

The partners worth keeping won't be the ones who say "yes, understood". They'll be the ones who ask hard questions and push back.

Is your business still running on time & material?

Upwork is testing a new way to hire: same-day, with a timer.

It’s called Upwork Now. Clients see it as “Hire Now”, and freelancers see it as “Work Now”. 

It’s currently in beta, so only a limited group of clients and freelancers can use it.

How it works for clients

→ Post a job with the Hire Now toggle turned on
→ A countdown timer starts
→ Uma, Upwork’s AI work agent, invites top-fit freelancers who are active right now
→ Applications come in live, and you hire within the timer window
→ If the timer ends with no hire, the job becomes a standard Upwork job and stays open

What freelancers agree to
→ Reply to invites and messages within 5 minutes, or the session ends
→ Start work the same day if hired

What clients should know

1).   A clear job post matters more than ever. Scope, deadline and budget help the AI invite better-fit freelancers.

2).   Keep a payment method or positive balance on your account. It is needed to send offers and messages.

3).   Due dates in the job post are informational unless they are agreed in the contract, so confirm timelines in the offer.

4).   Automatic matching does not guarantee that a recommended freelancer is available, qualified or interested.

5).   As a beta, Upwork can change or pause the feature at any time.

Fast hiring only works when both sides are responsive and the brief is clear.

I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.

"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"

I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."
He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.

That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:
Send request → check status code → check response body
What seniors answer:
🔹 Contract validation across consumers
🔹 Schema drift detection
🔹 State injection to remove UI dependency
🔹 Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
🔹 Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail
The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.
Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.
It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.
What was your "I didn't know what I didn't know" API testing moment?

Crossing $100M doesn’t mean your GTM foundations are solid. Often it means strong demand never forced you to test them.

A channel that works. A sales motion that delivers. You keep hiring salespeople, partner managers and marketers. Revenue keeps growing.

Then growth slows.

Macro conditions, competition and shifting demand explain part of it. The harder question is whether your GTM has kept up with the business you’ve built.

By the time a slowdown shows up in revenue, the cracks are months old.

What I’d look at:
1. Detect problems earlier.
Track pipeline quality, win rates, sales cycles, discounting, rep productivity and expansion by segment and geography. Aggregate numbers hide where the business is weakening.

2. Reduce channel dependence.
Add channels where buyer behaviour and unit economics support them. At Freshworks, rather than keep funding the low-segment prospects we’d been acquiring, we built outbound and events to reach mid-market buyers.

3. Revisit the market you can actually serve.
A large TAM doesn’t justify more territories. Prioritise segments and locations on product fit, customer urgency, implementation capacity and cost of coverage.

4. Keep upgrading how your teams sell.
Invest in coaching and practical uses of AI. Have people experiment, measure results and share what works. Make learning part of the operating rhythm.

5. Keep testing the offer.
Packaging, pricing and promotions should evolve with customers. Judge them on conversion, margin, adoption and retention.

6. Connect the customer journey.
Sales, implementation and customer success need a shared view of outcomes. What happens after the contract is signed drives renewals and expansion.

Before approving the next round of GTM hiring, ask:
Do we know where growth is weakening, and do we have evidence that more headcount will fix it?

The 2026 State of Data Engineering report confirms what I see in production every day: the role is bifurcating. One path leads toward platform engineering, where you build the infrastructure that others use. The other path leads toward workflow automation, where the engineer becomes the orchestrator of agents that write and execute pipelines autonomously. The teams that will thrive are the ones that embrace both, but with a clear architectural boundary between them.

The most non-obvious insight from the latest trends is that the hardest problem in data engineering is no longer scale, cost, or even quality. It is predictability. As AI assistants generate more of our pipeline code, the failure mode shifts from "this query is slow" to "this pipeline silently consumed 3x the expected budget because an agent optimized for speed over cost." The winning teams are not the ones with the fastest data platforms; they are the ones with the most deterministic cost models for non-deterministic workloads.

Another structural change is the maturation of platform-owned infrastructure. In 2025, the debate was centralized vs. decentralized data teams. In 2026, the debate is over who owns the governance contract. The teams that are winning are embedding cost, quality, and compliance policies directly into the pipeline deployment pipeline, not layering them on after the fact. This is not a tooling problem; it is a design philosophy problem. If your platform team is still approving data access via tickets, you are already operating at a structural disadvantage.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to write ETL scripts or tune Spark configurations. I am seeking a problem where I can design the platform governance layer, the cost-control frameworks, and the validation contracts that make autonomous data pipelines predictable at scale. If your team is struggling to transition from human-in-the-loop to agentic workflows without losing control of cost and quality, I want to hear about the specific compliance requirements and latency targets you are facing.

What is the one policy in your current data platform that, if codified as a CI/CD gate, would eliminate your most common cost overrun?
